lesson.title: Read a date without guessing

steps.headline: A date written as text is ambiguous until you state its format.

lead.text: 03/04/2026 could be 3 April or 4 March. format='%d/%m/%Y' says the first field is the day (%d), the second the month (%m) and the last the year (%Y).
Say the format. Do not let the software guess.
The format string decides which field is the month. Read the fields in the order the format lists them.

reveal.text: You followed the format, not a regional habit. %d came first, so the first field was the day and the middle field the month.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['03/04/2026'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%d/%m/%Y')

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['03/04/2026'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%m/%d/%Y')

steps.headline: With format='%Y-%m-%d' and errors='coerce', how many of '2026-06-31', '2026-07-01' and '2026-07-02' fail to parse?

lead.text: errors='coerce' turns anything it cannot read into a missing date, instead of stopping with an error.

workedSteps.text: Check each date against the calendar. June has 30 days, so June 31 does not exist.
The coerced result for the invalid date is a missing date.
The other two are real dates. Count the failures.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['2026-02-28', '2026-03-01'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%Y-%m-%d', errors='coerce')

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['2026-02-30', '2026-03-01'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%Y-%m-%d', errors='coerce')
invalid = dates.isna().sum()

steps.headline: With format='%Y-%m-%d' and errors='coerce', how many of '2026-02-30', '2026-03-01' and 'bad' fail?

workedSteps.text: February 2026 has 28 days. How many of the first two entries are real dates?
'bad' is not a date at all. How many of the three entries fail to parse?

steps.headline: An epoch number counts time from 1970-01-01, and unit says what one step means.

lead.text: Unix timestamps count from 1970-01-01 UTC. The number alone does not say whether it counts seconds or milliseconds, so pass unit='s' or unit='ms'.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series([0, 60]), unit='s', utc=True)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series([0, 60]), unit='ms', utc=True)

lead.text: With unit='s', each epoch step is one second. Subtract two offsets to get the seconds between them.

reveal.text: Both offsets counted seconds, so their difference was seconds too. You then divided by 60 to get minutes.

lead.text: Subtracting two timestamps gives a duration, and .days reads its whole days. The .dt accessor reads calendar fields such as the month from a column of dates.

reveal.text: The calendar counted the days left in February and then added the days into March. Subtracting dates handles month lengths for you.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(['2026-04-02', '2026-05-03']))
months = dates.dt.month

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(['2026-04-02', '2026-04-05']))
days = (dates.iloc[1] - dates.iloc[0]).days

lesson.orientation: Parse known date formats, retain invalid-date evidence and state epoch units.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: An invoice is dated 03/04/2026. In the UK the first number is the day. In the US the first number is the month.

intro.promise: By the end you'll parse a date with a stated format, count the dates that fail, and convert epoch numbers with the right unit.

recap.keyIdea: State the date format, count the dates that fail to parse, and say the unit of an epoch number before you convert it.

blocks.text: You read 03/04/2026 as month 4 under the day-first rule. You found 2 failures among three entries, and 4 days between 26 February and 2 March.

recap.nextHook: Next: summarise the right observations with means, medians and groups.

questions.prompt: Parse '05/09/2026' with format='%d/%m/%Y'. What month number results?
hints: Follow the format rather than a regional guess.
%d is the day and %m is the month.
Read the middle field as the month.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The format reads day 05 and month 09, so the month is 9.

questions.onCorrect: 9. The format reads day 05 and month 09, so the month is September.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the day. The format puts the day first and the month second.

questions.prompt: How many of the three entries fail to parse?
hints: Check calendar validity as well as the layout.
An impossible day and plain text both fail.
Count the entries that cannot become dates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: February 30 and bad cannot be parsed as valid dates, so both become NaT.

questions.onCorrect: 2. February 30 and 'bad' cannot be dates, so both became missing.

misconceptions.feedback: Both an impossible date and plain text fail the parse.
March 1 is a real date in the right format.

questions.prompt: Which parameter distinguishes an epoch count in seconds from one in milliseconds?
hints: The number alone does not give its scale.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: unit tells pandas how to interpret the numeric offset from the epoch.

questions.onCorrect: unit. It tells pandas how to read the number: seconds, milliseconds or another step.

misconceptions.feedback: axis chooses rows or columns in array and table methods, not a time scale.
sheet_name selects a worksheet when reading Excel files.

questions.prompt: What is the result of coercing an invalid datetime?
hints: Coercion records a failed parse as missing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: NaT marks the missing datetime. It does not supply a valid replacement date.

questions.onCorrect: NaT, a missing date. It does not invent a replacement date.

misconceptions.feedback: A duration is a different kind of value. A failed parse is simply missing.
pandas never substitutes today's date. It marks the entry missing.

questions.prompt: How many seconds separate epoch offsets 120 and 300 when unit='s'?
hints: Subtract the offsets in the same unit.
Both offsets use seconds.
Take the earlier offset from the later one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both offsets use seconds, so the elapsed time is 300 − 120 = 180 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: 180. Both offsets count seconds, so subtracting gives the gap in seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two offsets. Subtract the earlier from the later.

questions.prompt: How many days separate 2026-06-02 and 2026-06-07 at the same time of day?
hints: Take the earlier date from the later date.
The times of day are equal.
Count the midnights between the two dates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The later date is five days after the earlier one.

questions.onCorrect: 5. The later date is five days after the earlier one, since the times of day match.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts both end dates. A difference counts the gaps between them.

hints: Which part of the date is the month?
The date is written year, month, day.
Read the middle field as a number.
questions.prompt: What does the .dt.month accessor give for the date 2026-11-15?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The date is in November, month 11.

questions.onCorrect: 11. The accessor reads the calendar field directly, so no format guessing is needed once the date is parsed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the day of the month.

hints: Which field is the day for a UK reader?
The other field must be the month.
Read the middle field.
questions.prompt: As a UK reader, which month number is the invoice date?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Day first: 3 April, so the month is 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Day first means the middle field is the month, so it is April. The same text means March in the US.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first field, the day under the UK rule.
That is the year. The month is the middle field.

hints: Which letter comes first in the format, and what does it stand for?
questions.prompt: In the format '%m/%d/%Y', what is the first field?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: %m is the month and it comes first.

questions.onCorrect: The month. %m comes first in this format, so the first field is the month.

misconceptions.feedback: %d is the day, and it comes second in this format.
%Y is the year, and it comes last here.

hints: Does February have a day numbered 30?
Check the second date too.
Count the entries that exist on the calendar.
questions.prompt: How many of '2026-02-30' and '2026-03-01' are real dates?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: February 30 does not exist, and March 1 does.

questions.onCorrect: 1. February never reaches 30, so only March 1 is a real date.

misconceptions.feedback: February has only 28 days in 2026, so the first date does not exist.
The second date is a real date.

hints: Subtract the offsets in the same unit.
The difference is a number of seconds.
Divide it by the seconds in a minute.
questions.prompt: Epoch offsets 1000 and 4600 are read with unit='s'. How many minutes apart are they?
questions.onCorrect: 60. The offsets are 3600 seconds apart, and an hour holds 60 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap in seconds. The question asks for minutes.
That adds the offsets. Subtract the earlier from the later.

hints: How many days of February are left after the 26th?
Then add the days into March.
February 2026 has 28 days.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 26 to 28 February is 2 days, then 2 more reaches 2 March: 4 days.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Two days carry the date to the end of February, and two more reach March 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the day numbers, 26 and 2, as if they were in the same month.
February 2026 has 28 days, so there is one more day than that.
